Unofficial until approved by the

  MINUTES
  Regular Meeting
  ALHAMBRA CITY COUNCIL
  Council Chambers, 111 South First Street
  May 10, 2021
  6:00 p.m.

ROLL CALL: At 6:09 p.m., on Monday, May 10, 2021 the Alhambra City Council met in Council
Chambers.

PRESENT:  LEE, MAZA, MALONEY, ANDRADE-STADLER, PÉREZ
ABSENT:  NONE

Officials Present physically, via teleconference, and via video conference: City Manager
Binnquist, City Attorney Montes, Assistant City Manager Garcia, City Clerk Myles, Director of
Finance Lieu, Director of Public Works/ Utilities Ray, Director of Parks and Recreation Macias,
Director of Library LohGuan, Marketing and Communications Specialist Nguyen, Deputy
Director of Community Development Reynoso, Fire Chief Phelps, Police Chief Parra, Director of
Human Resources Ko

FLAG SALUTE:  Mayor Pérez

CITY CLERK REPORT - NOTICE NO. N2M21-54

The City Clerk reported that she duly gave notice of the regular meeting of the City Council
being held pursuant to the order of the Mayor in accordance with Section 54955 and 54956 of
the Government Code of the State of California.

PÉREZ:  Mayor PÉREZ requested that Council approve removing agenda Consent Item
Nos. 4 and 25 for early discussion before the presentation items due to the number of student
Public Speakers for both items.

  Vote:  Moved:  ANDRADE-STADLER  Seconded:  MALONEY
  Ayes:  LEE, MALONEY, ANDRADE-STADLER, MAZA, PÉREZ
  Noes:  NONE
  Absent:  NONE

READING OF ORDINANCE TITLES
Government Code Section 36934 requires that all ordinances be read in full prior to City Council
taking action on the ordinance. By listing the ordinance title on the Council agenda, Council may
determine that the title has been read.

Action Taken:  On motion of Ms. LEE, seconded by Ms. ANDRADE-STADLER, the City
Council determined that the titles to all ordinances which appeared on this public agenda had
been read, and waived further reading. Hearing no objections, the Mayor so ordered.

CEREMONIALS

1.  PROCLAMATION: ASIAN AMERICAN NATIVE HAWAIIAN PACIFIC ISLANDER
  HERITAGE MONTH – F2M21-3

  The Alhambra City Council ratified the action of Mayor Pérez in proclaiming May 2021
  as Asian American Native Hawaiian Pacific Islander Heritage Month in Alhambra.

2.  COMMENDATIONS: SUPPORTER OF ALHAMBRA’S CATALYTIC CONVERTER
  THEFT PREVENTION EVENT – F2M21-3

  Mayor Pérez and the Alhambra City Council wished to recognize and thank Neil’s
  Express Automotive and Promax Motorsports for their generous support at the Catalytic
  Converter Theft Prevention Event hosted by the Alhambra Police Department on April
  24, 2021. Their support and help made it possible to have approximately 60 catalytic
  converters etched with license plate numbers of residents’ vehicles which would aid
  officers in the return of catalytic converters to the owners in the event they are stolen
  and recovered. The City of Alhambra appreciated the efforts of Neil’s Express
  Automotive and Promax Motorsports and their contribution to the safety of our
  community. Maribel BARNUEVO, representing Neil’s Express Automotive, accepted the
  commendation and thanked the City for their recognition.

3.  CERTIFICATES OF SERVICE: OUTGOING BOARD & COMMISSION MEMBERS
  WHO SERVED 8-YEAR TERMS – F2M21-3, F2M21-31

  The City Council, on behalf of the citizens of Alhambra, wished to recognize the City’s
  outgoing Board and Commission members that served full, 8-year terms, for their
  outstanding and dedicated service to the City of Alhambra.

  DEBRA GARCIA
  Planning Commission

  BETTY HANSON
  Board of Library Trustees

PUBLIC HEARING

4.  2021-2022 ANNUAL ACTION PLAN FOR CDBG AND HOME PROGRAMS – F2M21-
  38, N2M21-42, M2M21-48

  This was the time and place set by Notice No. N2M21-42 for the City Council to hold a
  public hearing to consider the proposed Community Development Block Grant (CDBG)
  and HOME funding for the City of Alhambra’s proposed 2021-2022 Annual Action Plan

  2
5-10-21
   and to receive comment pursuant to and in compliance with the Federal Department of
  Housing and Urban Development (HUD) pre-submission requirements. Assistant City
  Manager GARCIA delivered a staff report. For FY 2021-2022, HUD notified the City of its
  funding allocations: $967,943 in CDBG Funds and $569,254 in HOME Funds. These
  represented a decrease in CDBG funds of $46,168 (approximately -4.55%) and a
  decrease in HOME Funds of $94,671 (approximately -14.26%) from FY 2020-2021. On
  April 6, 2021 the Housing and Community Development Citizen Advisory (HCDA)
  Committee met to address the allocations and identify activities consistent with federal
  regulations, and in alignment with the City’s 2020-2024 Consolidated Plan. The following
  programs were proposed to be funded from CDBG and HOME during FY 2021-2022:

  CDBG Administration  $  168,589
  Fair Housing Services  $  25,000
  Housing Rehabilitation (Minor)  $  279,163
  Code Enforcement/Proactive Rental Inspection  $  350,000
  Public Services (Case Management)  $  145,191
  CDBG Total  $  967,943

  Administration  $ 56,925
  CHDO (New Construction)  $ 85,388
  Housing Rehabilitation (Major)  $ 426,941
  HOME Total  $ 569,254

  The HCDA Citizen Advisory Committee reviewed the one-year Action Plan as presented
  and voted unanimously to recommend approval to the City Council. The notice for this
  hearing and the 30-day public review of the 2021-2022 Annual Action Plan was
  published in the Pasadena Star News, La Opinion, and World Journal newspapers. The
  plan was also available for review at City Hall and on the City's website. No public
  comments were received at the time the staff report was published.

  Open Public Hearing:  Mayor Pérez opened the public hearing.

  Public Comment received via email on file in the City Clerk’s office:

  1) Chris Olson requested clarity regarding the reduction in funding.

  2) Shirley Tatsuno suggested that funding for Code Enforcement should be allocated to
  small mom and pop landlords who house low-income renters to help with
  renovations.

  Close Public Hearing:  After receiving public comment, Mayor Pérez closed the
  public hearing.

  Discussion: Councilmember LEE requested clarification regarding the decrease in
  funding and Ms. GARCIA provided an explanation regarding on the formula used for
  allocation by the Federal appropriation group. Councilmember ANDRADE-STADLER
  and Ms. GARCIA continued to discuss the reduction in funds, additional potential funds
  being considered by the State and Federal governments, and identifying more funds to
  assist those negatively impacted by COVID-19 as well as economic hardship. She went
  on to highlight the need to address racial inequality in government programs. Ms.

  3
5-10-21
   GARCIA further discussed the proposed proactive rental inspection program through
  Code Enforcement which could also assess property owner qualifications for property
  rehabilitation assistance with Ms. ANDRADE-STADLER. Councilmember MALONEY
  praised the Annual Action Plan and echoed Ms. Andrade-Stadler’s comments regarding
  potential additional funding and requested a report from staff regarding the new
  opportunities. Councilmember MAZA and City Manager BINNQUIST discussed the
  current qualifications for multi-unit dwellings to receive assistance. Mayor PÉREZ
  praised the Annual Action Plan and the Proactive Rental Inspection Program.

  Action Taken:  City Council approved the proposed 2021-2022 Annual Action
  Plan for the Community Development Block Grant (CDBG) and HOME programs and
  authorized staff to submit the plan to the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban
  Development (HUD). (M2M21-48)

  Vote:  Moved:  ANDRADE-STADLER  Seconded:  MALONEY
  Ayes:  LEE, MALONEY, ANDRADE-STADLER, MAZA, PÉREZ
  Noes:  NONE
  Absent:  NONE

City Council proceeded to Item Nos. 24 and 25 for discussion.

PRESENTATIONS

5.  RECEIVE AND FILE THE 2021-2022 ALHAMBRA STRATEGIC PLAN – F2M18-35

  Assistant City Manager GARCIA delivered a staff report. On March 11, 2021, the City
  Council and Executive Team held a full day planning session to update the City’s Annual
  Strategic Plan. Strategic planning helps guide the work plan of the City. Further, it
  provides an important and effective way for the City Council to identify strategic goals
  and priorities to move Alhambra forward through work undertaken by the City’s
  Departments under the oversight of the City Manager. During the City’s strategic
  planning session, a total of 42 objectives were identified and retained under the following
  13 goals: 1. Expand Affordable Housing; 2. Increase Economic Development; 3.
  Enhance Green Space; 4. Implement Historic Preservation Ordinance; 5. Develop Shorb
  Plan; 6. Recruit and Retain Police Officers; 7. Secure Grants; 8. Improve Transportation
  and Mobility; 9. Improve Sustainability; 10. Evaluate Boards & Commissions; 11.
  Modernize Services; 12. Continue Community Outreach; 13. Address Lifestyle
  Enhancements. Following the distribution of this Strategic Plan to the Council, staff
  requested Councilmembers numerically prioritize each objective. Staff would then
  aggregate the various rankings to determine the Council’s highest priorities and bring the
  prioritized Strategic Plan back to the Council for final approval.

  Public Comment received via email on file in the City Clerk’s office:

  1) Sean McMorris wrote to request more progressive goals from the Strategic Plan.

  2) Lewis McCammon wrote to request more public input regarding Affordable Housing
  and Economic Development regarding East Main Street.

  4
5-10-21
   Discussion: Council expressed gratitude to staff and their work in codifying the various
  discussion points from the Strategic Planning session into a comprehensive list of
  priorities. Councilmember ANDRADE-STADLER requested that all policies and practices
  consider working towards racial equity and remove biases and barriers that historically
  and systematically marginalize communities of color to ensure that all people are
  healthy, prosperous, and can fully participate in civic life.

  Councilmember MALONEY made suggestions to clarify the priority list and discussed
  the prioritization methods with City Manager BINNQUIST. He further clarified certain
  points from the priority list for staff to update the list.

  Councilmember LEE stressed the importance of affordable housing and economic
  development in light of the negative impact of the COVID-19 pandemic, community
  outreach to non-English speaking residents and business owners, expanding
  greenspace, historic preservation as a means of entertainment, and securing grant
  opportunities for regional projects with neighboring cities.

  Councilmember MAZA also stressed the importance of affordable housing, economic
  development, streamlining permit system to assist new businesses, extending outdoor
  dining permits to assist economic recovery of small business, and creating design
  guidelines for multi-family properties.

  Mayor PÉREZ supported all additions mentioned by Council and made additional
  suggestions to improve the City’s pursuit of active transportation grants such as the
  creation of a Vision Zero Plan or a Road Safety Plan, consider the creation of a Safe
  Routes to School Plan or seeking grant funding for the Downtown Corridor, prevent
  displacement from transportation systems, explore a just cause eviction ordinance and a
  rent stabilization ordinance, and adopt a resolution in support of active transportation.
  She went on to suggest a program for the Library to provide assistance and outreach to
  businesses in language, a minimum wage ordinance for large corporations in Alhambra,
  adopting a Resolution to ban fracking in Alhambra, and an assessment of the mayoral
  rotation.

  Mr. MALONEY supported Ms. Pérez’s suggestions to improve grant opportunities. Ms.
  ANDRADE-STADLER also supported Ms. Pérez’s suggestions and highlighted the
  greenspace possibilities at the 710 stub. She went onto thank CALTRANS, Senator
  Rubio, Assemblyman Tran, and the residents for their efforts to clean the leftover
  materials along the 710 corridor. Mr. MALONEY also discussed the upcoming Virtual
  Town Hall meeting regarding the 710 corridor and stub and agreed with Ms. Andrade-
  Stadler’s suggestions. Council continued to discuss the 710 stub.

  Action Taken:  City Council received and filed the 2021-2022 Alhambra Strategic
  Plan.

6.  COUNCIL DIRECTION ON APPROVAL OF CONTRACT FOR FY 2021-2022 WITH
  THE ALHAMBRA CHAMBER OF COMMERCE – F2M21-43, F2M1-51, C2M21-25,
  M2M21-55

  Director of Parks and Recreation MACIAS delivered a staff report and introduced
  presenter Sharon Gibbs, Executive Director of the Alhambra Chamber of Commerce.

  5
5-10-21
   The City has contracted with the Chamber of Commerce for many years to conduct
  promotional activities on behalf of the City. Staff believed the services proposed for FY
  2021-2022 were essential to maintaining active communication lines with the business
  community and encouraging partnerships within the City. The Alhambra Chamber of
  Commerce requested an increase in allocation from $111,925 to $120,000. The
  Chamber of Commerce would add programs, such as a Commercial Brokers/Developers
  round table to help with vacancies and a Valley Boulevard Committee to identify better
  ways to revitalize the West Valley boulevard corridor, to the scope of work. The last
  increase in allocation of funds to the contract was in 2009. Staff sought direction from
  the Council on the approval of a contract for FY 2021-2022. Ms. GIBBS delivered a
  PowerPoint presentation of a summary of activities provided by the Alhambra Chamber
  of Commerce, which is on file in the City Clerk’s office.

PÉREZ:  Mayor Pérez left Chambers at 9:06 p.m., and returned at 9:09 p.m. during the
  presentation by Ms. Gibbs.

  Public Comment:

  1) Suzi DUNKEL-SOTO, President of the Alhambra Chamber of Commerce spoke in
  favor of the contract and outlined the various programs and services provided by the
  Chamber.

  2) Jon TI spoke against the contract and emphasized the more important needs for
  residents such as rental assistance, support for essential workers, and funding youth
  food programs.

  3) Lewis MCCAMMON noted differences between the PowerPoint presentation and the
  staff report and discussed the need for resident input regarding the revitalization of
  West Valley Boulevard. He discussed past opposition from residents for the
  proposed project on 801 E. Main St. He continued to discuss the need for resident
  input and referred to the Citizen Satisfaction Survey.

  Public Comment received via email on file in the City Clerk’s office:

  The following people wrote in favor of the contract:

  1) Cindy Ho, representing Office of David San Ho, Farmers Insurance
  2) Joanna Vargas, representing Jayvee Empire, Inc.
  3) Robert Fukui, representing High Point Marketing
  4) Helen Romero Shaw, representing the Southern California Gas Company
  5) Evike Chang, representing Evike.com
  6) Michael Derger, representing Academy of Special Dreams Foundation
  7) William R. Manis, representing San Gabriel Valley Economic Partnership
  8) Jerry Ruiz, representing the Academy of Special Dreams Foundation
  9) Jewelyn Co, representing Cokreate
  10) Valarie R. Gomez, representing the Alhambra Rotary Club
  11) Pinki Chen
  12) Brian Canseco-Chan
  13) John Bwarie, representing Alhambra Main Street Alliance
  14) A-Sha Foods USA Co., Inc.

  6
5-10-21
   15) Sister Kathleen Callaway, SNJM, representing Ramona Convent Secondary School
  The following people wrote against the contract:

  1)  Melissa Michelson
  2)  Michael Lawrence
  3)  Chris Olson
  4)  Efren Moreno, Jr.
  5)  David Bond
  6)  Cliff Bender
  7)  Eric Guarin

  Discussion: Councilmember MAZA discussed the last audit of the Alhambra Chamber
  of Commerce for fiscal years 2018 and 2019 with City Manager BINNQUIST.
  Councilmember MALONEY thanked the public for their comments. He requested the
  results of the most recent audit be included in the next staff report. He discussed the
  events hosted by the Chamber of Commerce and the participation and promotion of
  local small business owners, including women and people of color, rather than large
  corporate entities. He stated that he did not see the need to discontinue this contract and
  that the city should continue to encourage small businesses. He supported the contract
  and emphasized the oversight of the contract as well as funding sources for other social
  programs.

  Councilmember ANDRADE-STADLER thanked Ms. GIBBS and the Chamber of
  Commerce for their efforts to support local businesses during the pandemic, their focus
  on the Valley Boulevard focus group, and for the encouragement of outdoor dining
  arrangements for local restaurants to comply with COVID-19 related restrictions. She
  stressed that support of bills which benefit small businesses was not a partisan issue
  and that small businesses were essential for local economies. She requested that the
  Chamber consider information workshops to educate business retailers about the
  Tobacco Licencing Program. She continued to praise the student internship program
  and further suggested that the Chamber consider donating to the Alhambra Rose
  Parade Float Foundation Fund for the Tournament of Roses Parade Float.

  Councilmember LEE briefly discussed the variety of programs offered by the Chamber of
  Commerce. She requested that all informational flyers and materials provided by the
  Chamber be distributed in multiple languages and suggested that the Chamber maintain
  an inventory of which primary languages local business owners speak. She offered
  support of the Valley Boulevard discussions and stressed the importance of including
  input from residents. She encouraged ongoing public forums to receive feedback and
  insight from all community stakeholders. She went on to discuss the Chamber’s support
  of the Lift program with local schools, and questioned the appropriateness of the City
  reimbursing this program as it did not have a direct benefit to the City and Alhambra
  Unified School District already received funding for the program. She suggested that this
  provision could be left out of the contract.

  Mayor PÉREZ expressed appreciation for the way the report focused on the many retail
  business vacancies and spoke regarding her meetings with Ms. Gibbs and Ms. Dunkel-
  Soto regarding this matter. She addressed the public comment from local business
  owners and highlighted their numerous contributions to the community as well as ways
  of bringing progressive policies and ideas into their business models. Ms. PÉREZ and
  Ms. GIBBS discussed the reasons for the contract increase, the added programs to the

  7
5-10-21
   scope of work, the additional funds received by the Chamber and the decreased
  membership dues during the pandemic. They continued to address concerns regarding
  participation of non-chamber members and distribution of materials in multiple
  languages. Ms. PÉREZ and Ms. BINNQUIST discussed the audit process for the
  Chamber of Commerce contract as well as the last audit conducted in March 2020.

  Councilmember MAZA thanked the public for their comment and the ability to clarify
  certain points during discussion. He stressed the need to support the business
  community during the economic hardship of the COVID-19 pandemic. He echoed
  support for the Chamber of Commerce and highlighted the efforts of the Chamber to
  support the business community during the pandemic.

  Mr. MAZA motioned for approval, which was seconded by Ms. ANDRADE-STADLER.
  Ms. LEE requested an amendment to delete Item No. 11 from the contract regarding the
  $1,000 for the Lift program. Council discussed Ms. Lee’s amendment, but Mr. MAZA did
  not support the amendment so it was not included in the motion.

  Action Taken:  City Council awarded a contract to the Alhambra Chamber of
  Commerce, subject to final language approval by the City Manager and City Attorney, in
  an amount not to exceed $120,000 for FY 2021-2022; and, directed staff to undertake
  the steps necessary to finalize Council’s action. (M2M21-55)

  Vote:  Moved:  MAZA  Seconded:  ANDRADE-STADLER
  Ayes:  LEE, MALONEY, ANDRADE-STADLER, MAZA, PÉREZ
  Noes:  NONE
  Absent:  NONE

7.  DISCUSSION ON THE RESTRUCTURING OF THE DESIGN REVIEW BOARD, HCDA
  CITIZEN ADVISORY COMMITTEE AND ENVIRONMENTAL COMMITTEE – F2M21-36

  Assistant City Manager GARCIA delivered a staff report. On February 22, 2021, the City
  Council received public comment and a request from staff for further direction on the
  possible restructuring of the City’s boards, committees, and commissions pursuant to the
  Council’s Strategic Plan and the goals of enhancing communications between Council
  and the residents through the role of resident volunteers and creating a more efficient
  and effective approach to board/committee/commission business. The Council received
  information on the City’s ten commission groups, including their composition, purpose,
  and frequency of meetings. In addition, the Council heard comment regarding potential
  for overlap of work for select groups. In some instances, the original scope of the work
  as described in the Municipal Code is no longer applicable and/or is no longer in concert
  with what’s needed today. Following public comment and Council discussion of the
  matter, the Council directed this item return at a later date with staggered review.
  Following public comment and Council discussion of the matter, the Council directed this
  item return at a later date with staggered review. On April 12, 2021, the Council
  addressed changes to the Transportation Commission and the Civil Service
  Commission. Thereafter, on April 26, 2021, the Council also reviewed the Library Board
  of Trustees, Parks and Recreation Commission, and the Arts and Cultural Events
  Committee. This evening, the focus was on changes desired for the City’s Environmental
  Commission, Design Review Board, and the HCDA Citizen Advisory Committee.

  8
5-10-21
   Public Comment:  Lewis MCCAMMON discussed the Alhambra Municipal Code
  sections regarding the HCDA Citizen Advisory Committee and requested that the HCDA
  Citizen Advisory Committee review programs such as the Inclusionary Housing
  Ordinance, monitor the implementation of such programs, review the City’s Regional
  Housing Needs Assessment goals, more closely review the implementation of the
  proactive Code Enforcement goals, have members initiate their own meeting times if the
  Committee will no longer meet monthly, and require other departments to provide any
  additional requested information to the Committee.

  Discussion: Councilmember MALONEY first discussed changes to the Environmental
  Committee such as changing the name to the Environmental and Sustainability
  Commission, review and advise on new programs the City might be consider, hear
  presentations as to best practices which Council may not be able to schedule, review the
  City’s membership in the Clean Power Alliance, and hold and conduct public hearings
  regarding the development of the City’s Sustainability Plan. He suggested that the
  commission retain 5 members and possibly expand to 10 and meet every other month.

  Mr. MALONEY suggested no changes be made to the Design Review Board. Regarding
  membership requirements, he suggested non-restrictive language such as “strongly
  recommended” for qualifications. He also suggested that no changes be made to the
  HCDA Citizen Advisory Committee however he recognized that the Committee could
  provide further advice to Council regarding larger funding prospects.

  Councilmember ANDRADE-STADLER agreed with Mr. Maloney’s suggestions to the
  Environmental Committee and supported expanding to 10 members and bi-monthly
  meetings. She also agreed that no changes should be made to the Design Review
  Board. She agreed with Mr. McCammon’s comments and suggested that the HCDA
  Citizen Advisory Committee review the Consolidated Programs, the Inclusionary
  Housing Ordinance, and the Regional Housing Needs Assessment. She also agreed
  that the membership should consist of 10 committee members.

  Councilmember MAZA also supported Mr. Maloney’s proposed changes and
  suggestions. He also suggested including 2 youth members in the commission. He
  agreed that no changes be made to the Design Review Board, but added that a
  background in design should be encouraged. He made no suggestions for the HCDA
  Citizen Advisory Board.

  Councilmember LEE supported the Environmental Sustainability Commission, that they
  meet as needed, and review the activities of the Commission and continue to provide
  robust agendas for each meeting. Regarding the Design Review Board, she suggested
  that if professional backgrounds were not required for membership, then Board
  members should complete a degree of training to familiarize them with some of the
  specifics of design and architecture. She stressed the importance of the HCDA Citizen
  Advisory Committee, agreed to maintain 10 members, and suggested that Board
  members be more frequently briefed on current affairs. She agreed that the Board
  members could introduce their own topics for discussion. She went on to agree that the
  Board could meet as needed.

  Mayor PÉREZ agreed with her fellow Councilmembers’ comments, thanked Mr.
  McCammon for his comments and insights, and agreed with Mr. McCammon’s
  suggestions for the HCDA Citizen Advisory Board’s purview. She suggested that the

  9
5-10-21
   Board review the Regional Housing Needs Assessment goals, the implementation of the
  Inclusionary Housing Ordinance, and monitor the implementation of SB30 Housing
  Rights Act of 2018. She agreed to maintain the Environmental Committee membership
  of 5 members, that they review the Sustainability Plan funding if it becomes available to
  the City, that they review other State and Federal programs which the City could
  undertake and meet the goals of the Sustainability Plan.

  Action Taken:  City Council provided direction on any structuring changes to the
  City’s Environmental Commission, Design Review Board, and the HCDA Citizen
  Advisory Committee.

CONSENT AGENDA (Item Nos. 8 – 25)

All other items listed under the Consent Agenda, with the exception of Item Nos. 9, 14, 17, 19,
and 23, as well as previously removed #24 and 25, were considered by the City Council to be
routine and were enacted by one motion.

8.  ALHAMBRA ROSE PARADE FLOAT FOUNDATION – F2M21-39, M2M21-49

  At the April 12, 2021 City Council meeting, staff was authorized to enter into a two-year
  agreement with the Phoenix Decorating Company for the oversight and building of the
  Rose Float for $107,625 in year one and $110,315 in year two. Additionally, at this
  meeting, there was discussion amongst the Council to look into the possibility of initiating
  an Alhambra Rose Float Foundation with a 501(c)(3) non-profit organization status to
  support the City of Alhambra Rose Parade Float and accept financial donations from the
  community. Upon authorization, staff would initiate the filing of articles of incorporation
  and create proposed bylaws, subject to the approval of the City Manager and City
  Attorney.

  Discussion: None.

  Action Taken:  City Council authorized staff to initiate the process to create an
  Alhambra Float Foundation; subject to final language approval by the City Manager and
  City Attorney; and, directed staff to undertake the steps necessary to finalize the City
  Council’s action. (M2M21-49)

  Vote:  Moved:  LEE  Seconded:  ANDRADE-STADLER
  Ayes:  ANDRADE-STADLER, MAZA, MALONEY, LEE, PÉREZ
  Noes:  NONE
  Absent:  NONE

9.  RESOLUTION: ESTABLISH VOLUNTARY CONTRACTUAL ASSESSMENT
  PROGRAMS TO FINANCE OR REFINANCE RENEWABLE OR ENERGY EFFICIENT
  IMPROVEMENTS FOR PROPERTY OWNERS THROUGH THE CALIFORNIA
  STATEWIDE COMMUNITIES DEVELOPMENT AUTHORITY OPEN PROPERTY
  ASSESSED CLEAN ENERGY PROGRAMS – F2M21-40, R2M21-19

  The California Statewide Communities Development Authority (CSCDA) was created in
  1988 and is a joint exercise of powers authority, the members of which include

  10
5-10-21
   numerous cities and counties in the State of California, including the City of Alhambra.
  The CSCDA had two Open Property Assessed Clean Energy (PACE) programs to
  provide financing and refinancing to qualifying property owners for renewable energy,
  energy efficient, water efficient, and seismic strengthening improvements, electric
  vehicle charging infrastructure and other such improvements. The two programs, the
  CaliforniaFIRST Program and the CSCDA Open PACE Program, were entirely voluntary
  and were administered by a third-party program administrator. The programs worked by
  levying special assessments on a property which allowed a property owner to secure
  financing to install energy efficient improvements. In order establish these programs in
  Alhambra, the City Council must adopt a resolution of authorization. The CSCDA was
  allowed to provide these services under Chapter 29 of Division 7 of the Streets and
  Highway Code, and may issue bonds under this authority to finance or refinance energy
  efficient improvements. Prospective borrowers were advised to check with their current
  mortgage lender to ensure there are no restrictions to obtaining PACE financing.

  Public Comment:  Emily RAMEY, representing YGrene Energy Fund, spoke in favor
  of the Resolution and urged Council to add additional providers to future agendas for
  consideration in order to provide a truly competitive marketplace. She also addressed
  Mr. MAZA’s concerns from Council discussion regarding early aggressive sales tactics
  which have improved.

  Discussion: Councilmember ANDRADE-STADLER praised the resolution and
  encouraged support from Council. Councilmember MAZA expressed concerns with the
  resolution due his experiences as a real estate broker in which he has witnessed
  negative impacts against senior citizens and English as a second language property
  residents, such as increased property taxes from special assessments. He urged
  Council to reconsider adopting the resolution without more research. Ms. ANDRADE-
  STADLER and Mr. MAZA continued to discuss his concerns and the comments made by
  Ms. Ramey. He supported tabling discussion until Council could perform their due
  diligence by investigating all options. Councilmember MALONEY supported the
  substance of the Resolution and the intention, but considered Mr. Maza’s concerns and
  supported more discussion and research. He supported the consideration of other PACE
  programs and provided information from his meetings with the Clean Power Alliance to
  find qualifying residents for their rate payer assistance programs. Mayor PÉREZ
  admitted she requested this Resolution for consideration, and asked for more
  information regarding changes to state government oversight. City Attorney MONTES
  stated that he was not aware of changes made, but added that he could research the

23.  INTRODUCTION AND FIRST READING OF AN ORDINANCE ADDING CHAPTER
  6.18 TO THE ALHAMBRA MUNICIPAL CODE FOR MANDATORY ORGANIC WASTE

  18
5-10-21
   DISPOSAL REDUCTION – F2M20-39, O2M21-4787

  In September 2016, Governor Brown signed Senate Bill 1383 (S.B. 1383) also known as
  the Short-Lived Climate Pollutants bill into law. The legislation targets short-lived climate
  pollutants by focusing on reducing greenhouse gas emissions emitted from landfills. This
  bill established a target diversion rate of 50 percent by 2020 and 75 percent by 2025
  based on 2014 waste characterization levels. The State estimates that these reduction
  targets will result in an annual decrease of at least 4 million metric tons of greenhouse
  gas emissions by 2030. S.B. 1383 seeks to accomplish these target levels by recycling
  or diverting organic waste (organics) from being sent to landfills for disposal. CalRecycle
  estimates that two-thirds of the State’s entire waste stream is comprised of organic
  waste. Under S.B. 1383, local jurisdictions must adopt a mandatory and enforceable
  organics waste recycling ordinance. The law mandates that jurisdictions are required to
  provide organics collection and recycling services to all residential, both single family
  and multi-family dwellings, and commercial customers within their boundaries. For the
  purposes of S.B. 1383, organics are not only limited to food waste but also include green
  waste, wood waste, landscape and pruning waste, food-soiled paper waste, and fibers
  such as paper and cardboard. The proposed Ordinance is based upon a model
  ordinance provided by CalRecycle. The ordinance fulfills a major component of S.B.
  1383 requirements and will work in concert with the City’s new franchise waste hauler
  agreement to meet the additional provisions under State law. Jurisdictions that fail to
  pass a mandatory organics waste recycling ordinance by January 1, 2022, will face
  compliance actions from the State including administrative civil penalties up to $10,000
  per day.
  In addition to S.B. 1383 requirements, the proposed Ordinance will also ensure the City
  is in compliance with prior State laws regarding recycling and diversion mandates. Prior
  State legislation includes: A.B. 939 - California Integrated Waste Management Act; A.B.
  341 - Mandatory Commercial Recycling; A.B. 1594 - Use of Green Material as
  Alternative Daily Cover; A.B. 1826 - Mandatory Commercial Organics Recycling and
  A.B. 827 - Mandatory Commercial Organics Bins. All of these laws work in conjunction to
  divert as much waste as possible from being landfilled in order to offset the effects of
  climate change by reducing the levels of greenhouse gas emissions in California. The
  proposed ordinance, if approved, will become effective July 4, 2021, and will coincide
  with the commencement of the City’s new franchise waste hauler agreement. These two
  components will work in tandem to ensure the City is in compliance with S.B. 1383.

  At the February 22, 2021 and March 22, 2021 City Council meetings, the Council
  received presentations concerning the hazards of smoking and second-hand smoke.
  The City currently regulates smoking in certain areas in Chapter 9.18 of the Alhambra
  Municipal Code. After hearing the presentations, the Council gave direction to draft an
  ordinance modifying Chapter 9.18 to strengthen the restrictions on smoking. Based
  upon that direction, the attached ordinance would expand the prohibition on smoking to
  include outdoor dining areas and within 25 feet of same, within 20 feet of any entryway
  or operable window of a non-public building, public events, service areas, sidewalks,
  private apartment and condo common areas in complexes of at least 5 units (except in
  landlord designated areas at least 20 feet from other prohibited areas), within 20 feet of
  any vent into an enclosed area and any outdoor job or work sites (except in employer
  designated areas at least 20 feet from other prohibited areas). The ordinance included
  extensive findings concerning the hazards of smoking, based upon information provided
  by the Public Health Law Center’s and American Lung Association’s Law and Policy
  Partnership to End the Commercial Tobacco Epidemic. Additionally, the definition of
  smoking was updated to include the most recent state law code sections, as well as

   The City currently regulates smoking in certain areas in Chapter 9.18 of the Alhambra
  Municipal Code. The presentations also suggested that the Council consider adopting a
  tobacco retail license (TRL) program and ban the sale of flavored tobacco products.
  After hearing the presentations, the Council gave direction to draft an ordinance for a
  TRL and to prohibit the sale of flavored tobacco products. The attached ordinance: 1.
  Included extensive findings on the health hazards and concerns associated with
  smoking and flavored tobacco products; 2. Required all businesses in the City that sell
  tobacco products (including e-cigarette and vaping products) to obtain a tobacco retail
  license no later than January 1, 2022, and then to annually renew such license; 3.
  Prohibited the sale of flavored tobacco products and drug paraphernalia after July 1,
  2022 to allow existing retailers time to sell or otherwise dispose of their existing
  inventory; 4. Provided for penalties for violating any of the restrictions in the ordinance
  including, but not limited to, fines, license suspensions and revocations. Sale of tobacco
  products without a valid license is itself a violation of the ordinance.

Councilmember LEE requested that Council agree to agendize a discussion of Los Angeles
District Attorney Gascon’s policy on reform. She briefly discussed her research of the policies of
Hate Crime Enhancement and Low-Level Crimes and Life Sentencing. She expressed concerns
as to the wide-reaching implications of the Low-Level Crimes policy such as no jail time and no
criminal record, and would include offenses such as Driving Under the Influence, Possession of
Drugs, Low-Level Sexual Assault, Minor Assault without Injury, and Trespassing. She went on
to discuss the Hate Crime policy which would only allow enhancement in extreme situations and
expressed concerns as to how this would help the public. She reported on various cities which
had filed a vote of no confidence in the policy and continued to request that Council agree to
agendize discussion. City Attorney MONTES cautioned the rest of Council from further
discussion, informed them that Ms. Lee’s request must receive unanimous consent of the
Council to be agendized, and requested that Council simply indicate if they would support
discussion as requested by Ms. Lee. The request did not receive unanimous consent for
discussion and Ms. Lee agreed to draft her own letter regarding her concerns.
